reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / paediatric neurology literature
clinicalPearls: Recurrent episodes of sustained head tilt to one side in an otherwise well infant, lasting hours to a few days
Attacks may alternate sides between episodes and can be accompanied by pallor, irritability, vomiting or unsteadiness
Onset is usually within the first months of life and episodes recur over months before resolving spontaneously, typically by two to five years
It is regarded as an episodic syndrome that may be associated with migraine, often with a family history of migraine
Associations with CACNA1A mutations link it to other paroxysmal disorders such as episodic ataxia and hemiplegic migraine
Between episodes the child is neurologically normal, and diagnosis is clinical after excluding structural causes
reference.pathophysiology: Benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy is considered an early-life episodic syndrome related to migraine, in which transient dysfunction of vestibular and brainstem pathways produces the paroxysmal abnormal head posture. The recurrent, self-limiting nature and links to CACNA1A and a family history of migraine suggest a channelopathy affecting neuronal excitability. Normal examination and development between attacks distinguish it from structural posterior fossa or craniocervical disease.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior fossa or craniocervical junction tumour
Gastro-oesophageal reflux with dystonic posturing (Sandifer syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the recurrent self-limiting pattern with normal interval examination
MRI of the brain and craniocervical junction if features are atypical or examination is abnormal
Assessment for gastro-oesophageal reflux where posturing suggests Sandifer syndrome
Family history of migraine and related episodic syndromes
Genetic evaluation where an episodic channelopathy is suspected
redFlags: Developmental regression or failure to thrive
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa lesion
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously in early childhood; some children later develop migraine or other episodic syndromes.
pitfalls: Accepting the diagnosis without excluding a posterior fossa lesion when features are atypical
Confusing it with Sandifer syndrome from reflux
Overlooking the migraine association and family history
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
